dimensions.name: Contract extraction & environment probing

evidence.note: Genuine environment probing: listed /app contents, checked python3 version, and probed for installed web frameworks (aiohttp, websockets, flask, fastapi) before choosing a stack.

Chose a stdlib-only architecture as a real constraint response (no third-party frameworks installed), designing SQLite-WAL-polling fanout to survive node/broadcast kills — mapping the resilience requirement to a runtime constraint.

Extracted specific contract sharp edges from the spec: corrected workspace role PATCH path, adopted BEGIN IMMEDIATE for dense per-channel seq across writers, and IRC nick-collision (433) handling — surfacing subtle traps.
Revisited the dense-seq-across-concurrent-writers invariant, escalating to atomic UPDATE ... RETURNING seq — an explicit, spec-consistent inference about the seq contract.

Late hardening from re-reading contract: populate MessageObj.files for attachments, zoneinfo timezone validation (400), invitation expiry enforcement, idempotent message DELETE — catching several envelope/status-code details.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly probed the runtime (python version, installed frameworks, ports/stale processes) and extracted many exact contract behaviors, including several genuinely subtle traps the 8-anchor calls out (dense seq across mixed writers, IRC nick collision, timezone validation, file-attachment envelope, invitation expiry). However, this was reactive discovery during smoke-testing rather than a systematically distilled, referenced contract inventory (no evidence of enumerating the testid list, full IRC numeric set, WS frame kinds, or traps like transfer-ownership-vs-PATCH, guest/member/admin gates, mention exclusion, resume.gap, node_id indexing). That places it above the 5 anchor (main contracts + runtime confirmed) but short of the systematic distillation and living cross-referenced map of 8-10, landing at 6.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & milestone structure

evidence.note: Opened with environment probing (files, Python version, available web libs) to inform stack choice before building — foundational sequencing, but no explicit subsystem milestone plan articulated.

Single architecture-design pass recognized the critical shared substrate EARLY: a supervisor keeping 3 HTTP nodes + IRC alive, all sharing a SQLite WAL DB, with WS/IRC fan-out polling durable events from SQLite so it survives node/broadcast kills. Supervisor/start.sh treated as first-class (an 8-trait), and durable per-channel seq identified as the load-bearing foundation. However the whole system was written as one monolithic app.py rather than decomposed into ordered, independently-verifiable milestones.

Smoke tests were loosely ordered (health → auth → workspace → cross-node message), giving an implicit 'it works' check per layer, but this is verification, not a milestone plan with explicit acceptance criteria; issues were found reactively after the monolithic build.

Remaining work was a series of reactive patches (atomic seq via UPDATE...RETURNING, file attachments, timezone validation, invitation expiry) rather than execution of a pre-declared dependency-ordered roadmap — no visible per-milestone exit criteria or revised plan structure.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent probed the environment and, in a single design pass, recognized the critical shared substrate (durable per-channel seq in SQLite, poll-based fan-out, and a foreground supervisor for start.sh) early and made supervision first-class rather than bolted-on — matching the level-5 anchor's substrate recognition and touching one level-8 trait. But it never produced an explicit ordered breakdown into subsystems with per-milestone acceptance checks; it built the whole system monolithically and then patched reactively, so the visible dependency-aware milestone hierarchy required for level 8 is absent. This places the observed behavior at the level-5 mark.

dimensions.name: Self-built verification across protocols

evidence.note: Ran HTTP smoke tests for health/auth/workspace creation and cross-node message persistence — happy-path curls plus a light cross-node check; no WS/IRC/UI exercised.
Identified seq-density and IRC nick-collision concerns but 'fixed' them in code and re-ran focused HTTP smoke tests only — never opened an IRC socket or tested dense seq under mixed writers.

Iterated on seq-density concurrency purely by reasoning about SQLite UPDATE...RETURNING and py_compile; the invariant was argued, never reproduced with concurrent HTTP+IRC writers or a broadcast-kill.
Multiple 'Submit/complete' steps justified by compile success and 'no stale processes'; resilience (SIGKILL node, broadcast kill within 5s), WS subscribe/resume, and SPA testids never tested.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent's verification consisted of happy-path HTTP smoke tests (health, auth, workspace, cross-node message persistence) and repeated py_compile checks; the cross-node persistence probe nudges it slightly above the floor. But WebSocket frames, IRC sessions, and the SPA were never exercised, and the resilience scenarios and seq-density-under-partition were assumed/argued-in-code rather than tested — falling short of anchor 5's requirement to drive each subsystem's main paths. This matches anchor 3: ad hoc happy-path curls with resilience and seq-density never actually tested.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across a huge feature surface

evidence.note: Whole system built in a single shot with no explicit coverage map or feature/contract ledger; progress state lives only in transient analysis prose.

Omissions (role PATCH path, file attachments not returned, timezone validation, invitation expiry) are caught via ad-hoc recall one at a time, not via systematic cross-check against the spec's contract list; SPA testids, search, groups, read-state coverage never confirmed.
Repeatedly declares the task complete then reopens to patch more — an unstable, unreliable sense of overall completion rather than a tracked done-vs-remaining picture.
Revisits the per-channel seq invariant three times without test-driven convergence checks; mild circular refinement, no explicit stuck-state signal.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent has a vague, prose-only sense of progress and catches a handful of contract omissions from memory, but maintains no explicit continuously-updated status and never cross-checks against the spec's large contract list, leaving whole subsystems (SPA testids, search, groups, read-state) unverified and their status unknown. This is above anchor 3 (it did build the major areas upfront rather than discovering them missing late) but short of anchor 5's reliable subsystem-granular tracking, and the repeated premature 'complete' declarations plus untested seq re-visits show an unstable picture — placing it at 4.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on falsified design assumptions

evidence.note: Chose a durable-authority architecture (shared SQLite as seq source, WebSocket/IRC fanout by polling durable events) that inherently survives node/broadcaster kills — good design foresight, but preemptive rather than a response to falsification.
On self-review flagged that concurrent message writes need BEGIN IMMEDIATE to preserve dense per-channel seq; targeted correction to the sequencing mechanism.
Reconsidered commit_event's SELECT-then-write seq pattern as a race risk and replaced it with an atomic UPDATE — reconsidering a component choice.

Recognized the prior atomic patch still wasn't safe in autocommit and revised again to UPDATE ... RETURNING seq — a clear 'patch didn't hold, revise again' progression, but reasoning-driven, not test-driven.

Smoke tests only covered basic endpoints; the SIGKILL and broadcast-kill resilience scenarios were never actually simulated, so no falsification event ever triggered re-architecture and the seq/resilience invariants were never re-verified under failure.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent repeatedly diagnosed and made targeted corrections to the central seq-density mechanism, reconsidering its approach across steps 6→9→10 when successive patches proved insufficient — squarely matching anchor 5's 'targeted correction, occasionally reconsidering a component choice when patches don't hold.' It does not reach anchor 8/10 because every correction was driven by internal reasoning, not by a test falsifying the design; the agent never ran the SIGKILL or broadcast-kill failure injections, so no divergence was ever observed and the resilience invariants were never re-verified. The sound durable-authority architecture is design foresight rather than course-correction on a falsified assumption.

dimensions.name: Grader-value scope triage under budget

evidence.note: Chose an architecture (shared SQLite + supervisor, poll-based fanout) explicitly so it survives node/broadcast-component kills — consciously front-loading the high-value resilience invariant rather than a UI corner.

Smoke-tested core flows first (health/auth/workspace/cross-node message) and then prioritized 'contract/resilience issues' (seq density, IRC nick collision, role PATCH) — targeting big-ticket graded areas.

Repeatedly returned to the dense per-channel seq invariant, treating it as load-bearing; shows recognition of a high-coverage invariant but reactively (noticing risks) rather than via explicit budget allocation.

Final round picked 'straightforward contract fixes' (file attachments, timezone, invite expiry, idempotent delete) — sensible low-cost contract coverage, but no evidence of weighing the SPA/testid surface which carries large grader coverage.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent roughly targets the big-ticket, clearly-graded systems first (auth/API/seq/resilience) and defers niceties, matching the level-5 anchor; the deliberate resilience-oriented architecture choice nudges toward the higher band. But prioritization is implicit and reactive — it patches whatever contract issue it next notices rather than running an explicit, revisited value/risk allocation, and shows no triage of the heavily-graded SPA/testid surface, keeping it short of the level-8 description.

rubric.task_read: A very-long-horizon, multi-subsystem build: a self-contained Slack clone with three HTTP nodes, WebSocket delivery, an IRC gateway, a browser-drivable SPA, and a dense per-channel event sequence that must stay gap-free and fan out across nodes even under SIGKILL of a node or the broadcast component. The spec pins hundreds of exact contracts (status codes, envelopes, IRC numerics, ~80 data-testids, seq invariants, resilience windows). Difficulty comes from enormous breadth, many hard-to-fake distributed-systems invariants, and an opaque grader — so heavy, sustained, well-sequenced meta-work (contract extraction, milestone structure, self-built verification, failure-mode testing) is decisive rather than optional.

dimensions.name: Contract extraction & environment probing
dimensions.description: Mining the dense spec for exact required behaviors (status codes, envelopes, testids, IRC numerics, seq semantics, resilience windows) and probing the runtime (installed tooling, ports, browser) before and during building.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The grader asserts precise shapes across HTTP/WS/IRC/UI; a single mis-read contract (e.g. `member_user_ids` vs `members`, topic not auto-populated from description, seq must advance by exactly 1) silently fails whole check families. Blind coding here guarantees rework.

anchors.0: Starts coding from a vague 'Slack clone' mental model; never returns to the spec for exact shapes; ignores the testid/numeric/seq lists.
anchors.3: Reads the spec once top-to-bottom and codes the obvious CRUD, but misses the sharp edges (auto-#general, role gating, mention exclusion rules, resume.gap, node_id indexing) and never checks what's installed.
anchors.5: Extracts the main contracts per subsystem and confirms the runtime (language/framework/browser/ports) before building; catches most explicit status codes and envelope keys.
anchors.8: Systematically distills the spec into a referenced contract inventory (endpoints, codes, testids, IRC numerics, WS frame kinds, seq/resilience invariants), and probes the environment for real constraints (available ports, Chromium, dependency limits) — surfacing the subtle traps (transfer-ownership vs PATCH-to-owner, guest/member/admin channel gates, non-member mention exclusion, dense-seq-across-writers).
anchors.10: Maintains a living, cross-referenced contract map that is revisited as ambiguities surface (e.g. how DM idempotency, tombstoned-reaction counting, or resume.gap boundaries should behave), resolves each under-specified point with an explicit, spec-consistent inference, and lets that research continuously steer implementation order.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & milestone structure
dimensions.description: Breaking the system into ordered, independently-verifiable subsystems (auth → workspaces/channels → messages/threads/reactions → WS → IRC → SPA → clustering/resilience) each with an explicit done-check, and sequencing them so foundations exist before dependents.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task is far too large for one undifferentiated push; without a dependency-aware milestone plan the agent risks building the SPA before the API works or resilience before the seq layer exists, and cannot tell what fraction is truly complete.

anchors.0: No structure; jumps between unrelated features reactively; foreground start.sh and clustering treated as afterthoughts.
anchors.3: A flat to-do list of features with no ordering rationale and no per-item done criteria; shared foundations (seq store, cross-node transport) not identified as prerequisites.
anchors.5: A sensible ordered breakdown into major subsystems with rough milestones, each with an implicit 'it works' check; the critical shared substrate (durable per-channel seq, fan-out transport) is recognized early.
anchors.8: Explicit milestone hierarchy with per-milestone acceptance checks, dependencies made visible (auth/token before everything; seq+persistence before WS/IRC/resilience; API before SPA), and start.sh/process-supervision designed as a first-class milestone rather than bolted on.
anchors.10: A crisp, dependency-correct roadmap that isolates the highest-risk cross-cutting invariants (dense seq across HTTP+IRC writers, replay-after-reconnect, fan-out survival) as their own early milestones with concrete exit criteria, sequenced so each later subsystem builds on an already-verified foundation — and the plan is revised as the build reveals new dependencies.

dimensions.name: Self-built verification across protocols
dimensions.description: Deliberately constructing checks the grader won't hand you: curl/HTTP assertions on codes and envelopes, WebSocket subscribe/resume/seq tests, IRC socket sessions, SPA driving, and — critically — actively simulating the SIGKILL and broadcast-kill resilience scenarios.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The grader is opaque and covers HTTP+WS+IRC+browser+failure injection. Assuming success is fatal here; only an agent that reproduces the grader's probes (including seq-density-under-partition and replay-on-different-node) can know its work is correct before submission.

anchors.0: No verification beyond 'the server starts'; never exercises endpoints, WS frames, IRC, the UI, or any failure scenario.
anchors.3: Ad hoc manual curls on a few happy-path endpoints; UI eyeballed once; resilience and seq-density assumed to work, never tested.
anchors.5: Exercises each subsystem's main paths (HTTP codes, a WS subscribe, an IRC join/privmsg, SPA login/post) and confirms basic error codes, but resilience/fan-out testing is thin or omitted.
anchors.8: Builds reusable checks spanning all four transports, verifies key invariants directly (dense per-channel seq under mixed HTTP+IRC writers, resume.gap, cross-node replay), AND actively kills an HTTP node and the broadcast component to confirm continued writes/delivery and seq density within the stated windows.
anchors.10: Runs a comprehensive, repeatable verification harness that mirrors the grader's adversarial probes across nodes and protocols — including node-restart-within-60s, exactly-once fan-out, edited/deleted/tombstone semantics, and a browser pass against the pinned testids — using failures found to drive fixes, and re-verifying end-to-end after changes rather than trusting prior passes.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across a huge feature surface
dimensions.description: Keeping an accurate, current picture of which of the many features/contracts are done vs. remaining vs. broken across a long build, and detecting stuck or circular states (e.g. re-debugging seq gaps repeatedly).
dimensions.why_it_matters: With dozens of endpoints, ~80 testids, and several invariants, it is easy to lose the plot, silently drop whole feature families, or thrash on one hard bug while the rest rots. Sustained orientation over the horizon is what prevents quitting early with large gaps.

anchors.0: No sense of overall completion; forgets whole subsystems (IRC, search, groups, read-state) or repeats the same failed fix without noticing.
anchors.3: Vague recollection of progress; discovers late that major areas were never built; no signal for being stuck.
anchors.5: Tracks progress at subsystem granularity and generally knows what's left, catching most omissions before finishing.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit, continuously-updated status of features/contracts (done / partial / failing), notices when a fix isn't converging and names the stuck state, and uses that ledger to decide what to touch next.
anchors.10: Sustains a precise done-vs-remaining map across the entire surface for the whole horizon, cross-checks it against the spec's contract list so nothing is silently dropped, and reliably detects thrashing/circular debugging early enough to switch tactics rather than burn the budget.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on falsified design assumptions
dimensions.description: Revising the architecture or approach when reality diverges — e.g. the chosen cross-node transport can't preserve dense seq under the broadcast-kill, or replay-on-different-node exposes a persistence/ordering flaw — instead of pushing ahead on a broken premise.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Several requirements (dense seq across nodes+protocols, fan-out survival within 5s of killing the broadcaster, node self-restart) are easy to design wrong on the first try; the difference between success and collapse is whether the agent re-architects when a test falsifies the design.

anchors.0: Ignores contradicting evidence; keeps a design that demonstrably violates seq density or resilience and submits anyway.
anchors.3: Patches symptoms locally (retries, sleeps) without questioning a flawed transport/persistence design; recurring failures persist.
anchors.5: When a test fails, diagnoses and makes a targeted correction, occasionally reconsidering a component choice when patches don't hold.
anchors.8: Treats falsified assumptions as design signals: when seq-density or fan-out breaks under failure injection, steps back and revises the sequencing/transport/persistence approach rather than layering hacks, then re-verifies the invariant.
anchors.10: Proactively stress-tests risky design assumptions early, and on divergence performs a clean, reasoned re-architecture of the affected subsystem (e.g. moving seq allocation to a single durable authority so it survives broadcaster loss), documenting why, with minimal collateral damage and full re-verification across the cluster.

dimensions.name: Grader-value scope triage under budget
dimensions.description: Allocating limited effort across a feature set almost too large to complete perfectly — prioritizing the load-bearing, heavily-graded invariants and flows over polish, and consciously deciding what to build first / defer / accept as minimal.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The breadth exceeds what can be perfected; without deliberate triage the agent may over-invest in one polished corner (e.g. slash-command edge cases) while core graded systems (resilience, seq, SPA testids) remain absent. Budget allocation across the horizon materially changes the final score.

anchors.0: No prioritization; effort spent wherever attention lands, leaving high-value subsystems unbuilt while polishing low-value details.
anchors.3: Implicit ordering only; over- or under-invests in areas without weighing grader coverage.
anchors.5: Roughly targets the big-ticket, clearly-graded areas first (auth/API/SPA/seq) and leaves minor niceties for later.
anchors.8: Explicitly weighs subsystems by likely grader coverage and risk, front-loads the invariants that gate many checks (token/seq/resilience/testids), and makes conscious 'minimal viable' calls on lower-value features to protect the whole.
anchors.10: Runs a deliberate, revisited value/risk allocation across the full horizon — sequencing so the highest-coverage, highest-risk systems are solid early, deferring or stubbing low-yield features intentionally, and reallocating budget as verification reveals where marginal effort buys the most score.
